item.title: Chioma Ude Celebrates Women in African Cinema at AFRIFF 15 Dinner | See Photos
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Chioma Ude hosts an exclusive AFRIFF dinner with Chef Tolu Eros, honouring the women driving African cinema forward.

The post Chioma Ude Celebrates Women in African Cinema at AFRIFF 15 Dinner | See Photos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
For AFRIFF’s 15th anniversary, Chioma Ude made room for a different kind of celebration: an intimate dinner dedicated to the women shaping African cinema. The gathering brought together female filmmakers, producers and directors for an evening of fashion, good food and conversations about the industry they are helping to shape, with plenty of opportunities to catch up and connect outside the usual festival setting.

As founder and executive director of the Africa International Film Festival, Chioma established AFRIFF in 2010 to showcase African talent and create more opportunities for filmmakers to reach wider audiences. Fifteen years on, the festival has become an important platform for African cinema, making the dinner a fitting occasion to celebrate some of the women contributing to the industry.

The evening also came with a specially curated dining experience by Chef Tolu Eros whose multi-course menu brought West African flavours into a fine-dining setting. Alongside the conversations and fashion, the dinner offered guests a chance to enjoy good food and celebrate the women whose work continues to shape African storytelling.

item.title: 5 Trending Nollywood Movies to Add to Your YouTube Watchlist This Week
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
From 7 Years Silence and The River Remembers to Caught in the Cycle, User Friendly and Beyond Blood, these five Nollywood films feature stories of romance, betrayal, family conflict and suspense, now streaming on YouTube.

The post 5 Trending Nollywood Movies to Add to Your YouTube Watchlist This Week appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Official poster for The River Remembers starring Teniola Aladese and Taye Arimoro, streaming on Omoni Oboli TV.

Secrets have a way of coming out, family ties can get complicated, and love doesn’t always go according to plan. These are just some of the stories unfolding in this week’s Nollywood releases on YouTube. From psychological drama and riverine mysteries to corporate battles and family betrayals, here are five films bringing different stories to the screen.

7 Years Silence (Bolaji Ogunmola TV)

What happens when a web of long-kept secrets finally unravels after nearly a decade? 7 Years Silence follows a devoted wife who, after seven years of marriage and a painful struggle to conceive, discovers her seemingly perfect husband has been living a complete double life. As hidden motives and suppressed truths explode into the open, every character is forced to face the shattering fallout of a marriage built on an illusion.

This gripping emotional thriller features standout performances by BamBam (Bamike Olawunmi–Adenibuyan), Deyemi Okanlawon, and Teniola Aladese.

The River Remembers (Omoni Oboli TV)

Love and dark ancestral secrets collide in this haunting riverine drama. Newly engaged Morayo and Akindele travel to his hometown to celebrate their future, but beside a forbidden river, Morayo’s recurring nightmares begin to unearth a devastating truth. As painful revelations draw an unyielding line between their families, the couple is forced to choose between their dream together or losing each other to a past they never chose.

Produced by Nollywood powerhouse Omoni Oboli, the movie stars Taye Arimoro, Teniola Aladese, Kunle Omisore, Najite Dede, Olami Samuel, Bridget John, Oyetola Elemosho, Tolu Otebiyi, Paul Word, Taiwo Familoni.

Caught in the Cycle (Biodun Stephen TV)

Tackling heavy themes of trauma, broken trust, and survival, Caught in the Cycle delivers an intense psychological ride. The narrative centers on a gifted teenage girl whose life takes a terrifying turn after she is taken in by a wealthy couple promising her a brighter future. Instead of sanctuary, she finds herself trapped in a living nightmare of abuse, manipulation, and betrayal—ultimately leading to a shocking crime that forces her to fight with everything she has for her freedom and the truth.

Directed by Olubunmi Akingbola and produced by Biodun Stephen, the film relies on raw, high-stakes performances from an impressive cast starring Stan Nze, Angel Unigwe, and Leolidas Ewane.

User Friendly (RuthKadiri247)

High-stakes corporate greed meets unexpected romance in User Friendly. Following her father’s death, billionaire heiress Tenny (Ruth Kadiri) struggles to take charge of his business empire as alcohol abuse and poor choices make her a prime target for manipulative relatives. To protect her, her grandmother hires Morris (Maurice Sam), a firm bodyguard tasked with shielding her from family sabotage. As Morris helps her navigate the corporate snakes, their professional bond evolves into a deep romance that reshapes her future.

Helmed by Ruth Kadiri, the film stars Ruth Kadiri and Maurice Sam, alongside Fessa Okafor, Betty Ndidiamaka Okafor Ajoku, and Anthony Woode.

Beyond Blood (Uche Montana TV)

Closing out this week’s recommendations is Beyond Blood, a story that proves the people we trust the most can often become the source of our deepest pain. Driven by bitter betrayals, hidden motives, and a desperate craving for vengeance, the film examines how far someone will push past boundaries to make things right when blood ties turn toxic. It is a high-drama narrative packed with explosive family conflicts, emotional struggles, and unexpected twists.

Directed by Ben Cassie, the project relies on intense onscreen chemistry between Uche Montana and Nollywood veteran Emeka Ike alongside a dynamic supporting cast.

item.title: Nkanyeziyethu Malunga: The Zimbabwean Designer Preserving African Heritage Through Fashion
item.dc:creator: Bird
item.description:
Sebele feels that this work has applications beyond fashion, such as cultural tourism, research, and creative enterprise. Its significance stems from making indigenous knowledge visible, as well as demonstrating how it may be used to inform future research and commercial activities.

The post Nkanyeziyethu Malunga: The Zimbabwean Designer Preserving African Heritage Through Fashion appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
At her workshop in Bulawayo, Zimbabwe, Nkanyeziyethu Malunga crafted colour into fabric, using plants, tree bark and other natural materials gathered from the environment. Choosing a colour or designing a pattern is only one of the processes. Each material carries details on how it was gathered, prepared, and transformed, which Malunga is incorporating into contemporary fashion.

“My dyes are mainly extracted from plants such as mnyii and hibiscus. Although I also use many other plants, including tubers, that have properties suitable for dye extraction. I love hibiscus not only for its petals, which produce beautiful dyes, but also for its tea.”

The 37-year-old designer is challenging conventional notions about what defines a fashion collection and where creative knowledge originates. Through her clothing business, GANU, she transforms indigenous materials and skills into clothes and accessories, demonstrating how knowledge passed down through generations can inform modern design, provide opportunities for rural women, and conserve cultural practices.

Her method is based on teachings learned from her late maternal grandmother, Ngatsha Nkatha, who resided in Tsholotsho, a rural district in Zimbabwe. During the school vacations, Malunga and her siblings traveled from Bulawayo to visit grandma, witnessing as she turned sisal, sedge, and reeds into winnowing baskets.

“When I was a child, I often visited my grandmother in the village with my siblings. She was very dexterous with her fingers, and that passion eventually became mutual.”

Malunga started experimenting with fashion in her teens before launching Ganu in 2013. The name is derived from iganu, the Ndebele term for marula fruit, and represents her connection to local resources and African identity. Her creations blend basketry, crocheting, batik, and beadwork with natural dyes, leather, and other locally produced materials.

For Malunga, the importance of these materials goes beyond their appearance. Bamboo, sisal, reeds, and sedge are used in basketry, and she breeds Angora goats for their fur, which she straightens and dyes to make garments. Cowhide obtained from local abattoirs is softened in a tannery before being mixed into leather designs.

“I keep Angora goats for the fur needed in garment production. However, for raw materials such as cowhide, I usually source these from local abattoirs while sisal and tree barks are either harvested by me or sometimes extracted by colleagues I work with, who are based in the rural areas.”

Desmond Ntini, a cultural entrepreneur based in Bulawayo, sees Malunga’s work as part of a broader shift in how African history is perceived and used.

” Malunga is redefining the fashion industry by blending traditional African influences with contemporary creativity. Her work explains how our cultural identity can inspire modern designs while opening doors for sustainable fashion, business opportunities, and the celebration of African heritage.” Ntini said.

Her ventures also go beyond her own label. In 2024, she founded Matobo Goes Fashion And Beyond, working with Matobo women in partnership with Ekhaya-gaia, my beautiful home in Zimbabwe, and the Amagugu International Heritage Centre. The concept transforms traditional hut paintings into contemporary clothes.

The project addresses the issue of cultural preservation. Rain can remove paintings from traditional dwellings, putting communities at risk of losing patterns that are not often documented. Reproducing these designs on fabric provides another way to record and disseminate them, as well as introduce the patterns to audiences outside of the communities where they originated.

The initiative also provides opportunities for women to share their knowledge and engage in the interpretation of their cultural legacy. Rather than interpreting traditional decoration as something that solely belongs in rural dwellings, the concept incorporates it into a new context while maintaining its connection to the communities that created it.

This approach opens up the possibility of adding value to Zimbabwe’s resources and abilities rather than regarding them as apart from the official fashion sector.

Zimbabwe’s cultural and creative industries contributed an estimated US$2.7 billion to the country’s economy in 2024, equivalent to 5.92% of gross domestic product, according to a study whose findings were reported in June 2026. The sector accounted for an estimated 22,223 jobs.

Dr. Florence Sebele, a senior lecturer and acting chair of the Department of Art, Design, and Technology Education at the National University of Science and Technology in Bulawayo, studies indigenous knowledge in textile technology. She sees Malunga’s method as an opportunity to challenge assumptions about African creativity.

“By taking indigenous knowledge that has long been undervalued and transforming it into modern fashion, Malunga speaks to our identity, culture and heritage as Zimbabweans and also as Africans. Her work is a powerful reminder that we have so much to take pride in, while for the wider world, it challenges the dominant narrative of what fashion is and where innovation comes from, showing that authentic, rooted African knowledge has global relevance.”

That dilemma is especially important in an industry where African cultural references can be seen on international runways yet the expertise and people that support them receive little recognition. Malunga’s work begins with techniques and materials rooted in local culture and then adapts them for modern applications.

Sebele feels that this work has applications beyond fashion, such as cultural tourism, research, and creative enterprise. Its significance stems from making indigenous knowledge visible, as well as demonstrating how it may be used to inform future research and commercial activities.

Malunga’s grandmother died before she could pass on everything she knew, leaving Malunga to seek out other custodians of traditional skills.

“My grandmother’s death came early, before I could master everything on the use of indigenous knowledge in creating contemporary fashion. As a result, I have also learned to tap into the wisdom of various elderly women that I have come across since embarking on this journey.”

Her creations have been showcased on platforms beyond Zimbabwe, including the Durban Fashion Fair in South Africa in 2016. She was nominated for Outstanding Fashion Designer at the 2018 Bulawayo Arts Awards and has worked with markets in Ghana, Europe, and the United States. She displayed under the ZimTrade pavilion at the Zimbabwe International Trade Fair in April of this year, and the organisation’s SheExports initiative has helped her explore international markets.

However, the greater relevance of Malunga’s work rests in what occurs before a garment reaches a buyer. Plant dyes, basketry skills, traditional paintings, and rural women’s expertise all contribute to a creative process that bridges generations and creates new avenues for cultural expression.

“…we learn everyday, we learn as we go, and we learn from everyone,”Malunga reflected.

Malunga’s challenge is to ensuring that this expertise is retained, that the communities that contribute to it are acknowledged, and that the opportunities it offers extend beyond the runway.

Story Credit: Rapelang Immaculate Ncube for Bird Story Agency

item.content:encoded:
Carex, one of Nigeria’s leading personal hygiene brands, has successfully concluded its nationwide Everybody Wins Promo with a transparent Grand Finale Live Draw, rewarding loyal consumers and reinforcing its commitment to delivering value beyond personal care products.

The campaign, which ran from June 2026 to August 2026, attracted millions of consumers PAN Nigeria and rewarded winners with prizes worth over ₦400,000,000.

The Grand Finale Live Draw, held in Lagos, brought together consumers, media representatives, trade partners, regulatory officials, and other key stakeholders to witness the selection of the campaign’s grand prize winner through a transparent and independently supervised process. The event marked the culmination of months of consumer participation and engagement, further strengthening the connection between the Carex brand and its consumers.

Throughout the promotion, participants had multiple opportunities to win exciting rewards, including instant Recharge Cards, shopping Vouchers, and a brand-new Car. Over 90,000 consumers emerged as winners over the course of the campaign. The grand prize car winner, Faith Stephen from Ijebu Ode, Ogun State, emerged through the live draw process conducted in accordance with all applicable promotional and regulatory requirements.

Speaking at the event, Ifunanya Anwunah, Head of Category – Personal Hygiene, said:

“At Carex, we believe that the consumers who trust our products every day deserve to be appreciated and rewarded. The Everybody Wins Promo was created as a tangible expression of our gratitude for the loyalty and support we continue to receive from Nigerian families.“

The overwhelming participation and enthusiasm witnessed throughout this campaign demonstrate the strong connection consumers have with the Carex brand.

The promo was built on a simple promise: giving everyday consumers the opportunity to win meaningful rewards while enjoying the quality, care, and protection they have come to trust from Carex.

As a brand trusted by millions of Nigerians for their personal hygiene and care needs, Carex remains committed to developing initiatives that deepen consumer engagement, reward loyalty, and create memorable experiences for consumers across the country. The successful completion of the Everybody Wins Promo further underscores the brand’s commitment to putting consumers at the heart of everything it does.

About Carex

Carex is committed to winning the war against germs through a range of antibacterial products that support the health, hygiene, and wellbeing of consumers. Through innovative products and engaging consumer initiatives, Carex continues to build meaningful connections with families across Nigeria, delivering trusted products that help consumers live healthier and more confident lives.

item.title: History in Morocco! How Nigeria’s Flamingos Won the World Cup
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.category: FIFA U17 Womens World Cup Morocco 2026
item.description:
Nigeria’s Flamingos won the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco, defeating Japan 2–1 in the final to become the first African nation to lift a FIFA women's trophy.

The post History in Morocco! How Nigeria’s Flamingos Won the World Cup appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
The Flamingos celebrate on stage with green and white confetti as they lift the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy.

History was made in Rabat as the Flamingos of Nigeria conquered global football at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup. Under head coach Akeem Busari, the team executed an extraordinary seven-match campaign at the finals, overcoming an early setback to claim six consecutive victories and become the first African nation to lift any FIFA women’s international trophy.

Midfielder Oluebube Umejiaku earned individual recognition by winning the FIFA Golden Ball as the Player of the Tournament alongside Player of the Match honors in the final. The squad also displayed exceptional attacking breadth, scoring goals through eight different players across seven matches at the finals while registering over 100 goal attempts.

Oluebube Umejiaku poses with the FIFA Golden Ball and Player of the Match awards following Nigeria’s World Cup triumph.

Here is the match-by-match breakdown of how Nigeria navigated the African qualifiers, powered through the World Cup group stage, defeated multi-time global champions in the knockouts, and clinched the ultimate trophy in Morocco.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate becoming the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after defeating Japan 2-1 in Rabat.

Phase 1: The African Qualifying Journey

Nigeria entered the African U-17 World Cup qualifying campaign in the second round, establishing dominance in home-and-away aggregate ties across West Africa. The Flamingos opened their qualification run with an emphatic 5–0 away victory in Guinea, led by team captain Harmony Chidi’s first-half hat-trick alongside goals from Oluwakemi Adegbuyi and Mary Dunstan. They followed up with a 7–0 victory in the home leg in Ogun State to complete a 12–0 aggregate shutout.

The Flamingos celebrate on the pitch following their matchday four fixture at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

In the final qualifying round, Nigeria established a three-goal lead in Monrovia by defeating Liberia 4–1, thanks to a brace from Harmony Chidi and goals from Shakirat Moshood and Peace Effiong. Chidi then sealed a 2–0 second-leg win back home to finish the qualifiers with 12 goals and secure Nigeria’s ticket to Morocco.

Phase 2: Group B at the World Cup (Morocco)

Placed in Group B alongside Poland, Puerto Rico, and defending world champions DPR Korea, Nigeria had to battle through one of the tournament’s most competitive pools. The campaign started with a tight 2–1 loss to Poland in Rabat, putting pressure on the team to perform in their remaining fixtures. The Flamingos bounced back immediately with a 2–0 shutout victory over Puerto Rico to claim their first three points.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate their historic 3-1 Group B victory over defending champions DPR Korea in Morocco.

In their final group match, Nigeria produced one of the tournament’s biggest tactical upsets by defeating two-time defending champions DPR Korea 3–1. Goals from Oluwakemi Adegbuyi, Oluebube Umejiaku, and Kanyinsola Yusuf snapped DPR Korea’s long unbeaten regulation-time streak at the U-17 World Cup and sent Nigeria through to the knockouts at the top of Group B on head-to-head tiebreakers.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino presents the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy to Nigeria captain Harmony Chidi alongside CAF President Patrice Motsepe.

Phase 3: The Knockout Stages

Nigeria entered the expanded 16-team knockout rounds, defeating top-tier opponents from CONCACAF, CONMEBOL, and AFC. In the Round of 16, Nigeria put together a strong performance against Mexico, winning 2–1 through goals from Oluebube Umejiaku and Mary Dunstan. The quarter-final against Venezuela proved to be a tense affair, remaining scoreless until the 89th minute when Oluebube Umejiaku won a late penalty.

Nigeria captain Harmony Chidi in action during the Round of 16 as the Flamingos secured a 2-1 victory over Mexico in Morocco

Substitute defender Azeezat Oduntan converted from the spot to send Nigeria to the semi-finals. Facing South American champions Brazil in Rabat, Nigeria broke through in the 56th minute with a strike from Queen Joseph before forward Awawu Bashiru scored twice in the 71st and 80th minutes to lock in a 3–1 win and book Nigeria’s place in the final.

The Final: Nigeria 2–1 Japan

Played at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat, Morocco, Nigeria claimed the World Cup title with a 2–1 victory over Japan. Awawu Bashiru opened the scoring in the 39th minute with a long-range shot.

Two minutes after half-time, tournament MVP Oluebube Umejiaku doubled the advantage. Japan pulled a goal back through Fuki Ito in the 80th minute, but Nigeria defended their lead through stoppage time to secure the World Cup trophy.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate becoming the first African nation to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after defeating Japan 2-1 in Rabat.

The Flamingos react after earning a spot in the quarter-finals of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

Nigeria’s Flamingos celebrate on the field following their quarter-final win over Venezuela.

item.content:encoded:
As Africa accelerates its digital transformation journey, the conversation is no longer simply about adopting new technologies, it is now about ensuring they are deployed responsibly, governed effectively, and trusted by the people they serve. 

It is against this backdrop that the Eko Innovation Centre, in collaboration with the Lagos State Ministry of Innovation, Science & Technology, announces the 8th edition of the Art of Technology Lagos (AOT Lagos 8.0), scheduled to hold on Thursday, 3 December 2026, at the Landmark Event Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. 

Now in its eighth year, AOT Lagos has welcomed over 125,000 participants, hosted 340 speakers, delivered 262 keynote sessions, and generated more than 15 million engagements across 145 countries. More importantly, AOT Lagos has evolved beyond a conference into a platform for collaboration and policy development, contributing to landmark initiatives including the Lagos

Innovation Master Plan, Startup Lagos, the Talent Acceleration Masterplan, the Lagos Digital Service Portal, and the Lagos Digital Service Portal 2.0 (Chatbot Inclusive). 

This year’s theme, “Beyond Smart Cities: Tech Adoption × Ethics × Governance,” reflects one of the defining conversations of our time. As artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, connected services, and data-driven technologies continue to transform economies and societies, governments and businesses must ensure innovation is underpinned by transparency, accountability, inclusion, and public trust. 

Bringing these critical conversations to the forefront, AOT Lagos 8.0 will feature a distinguished line-up of technology leaders, policymakers, entrepreneurs, and global industry experts, including Dr. Bosun Tijani, the Honourable Minister of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, Sade Dada, Head of Public Policy, Anglophone West Africa at Meta, Engr. Abisoye Coker-Odusote, Director-General and Chief Executive Officer of the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), the Honourable Commissioner, Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology, Lagos State Olatubosun Alake and more. Their participation will bring diverse perspectives to the conference’s central conversations around responsible AI adoption, digital governance, smart infrastructure, the future of work, digital inclusion, and sustainable innovation.

Speaking on this year’s edition, Victor Afolabi, Founder of Eko Innovation Centre, said:

“Technology is changing faster than ever before, but sustainable progress depends on more than innovation alone. It requires responsible adoption, effective governance, and meaningful collaboration across the public and private sectors. AOT Lagos 8.0 provides a platform for the conversations, partnerships, and ideas that will help shape Africa’s digital future.”

This year’s conference will feature executive keynotes, policy dialogues, ministerial roundtables, technology exhibitions, startup showcases, investment engagements, and strategic conversations across eight thematic tracks covering:

  • AI, Ethics & Governance
  • Smart Infrastructure & Urban Innovation
  • Fintech, Regulation & Digital Economy
  • Future of Work & Talent Transformation
  • Digital Identity, Data & Cybersecurity
  • ClimateTech & Sustainable Cities
  • Civic Technology & Digital Inclusion
  • Startup Innovation & Investment

The conference will also host the 5th AOT Ecosystem Awards, recognising outstanding startups, ecosystem builders, policymakers, and organisations driving innovation and digital transformation across Nigeria and the African continent.

Building on seven successful editions, AOT Lagos 8.0 aims to strengthen public-private collaboration, inspire innovative solutions, encourage investment, and generate policy recommendations that support responsible technology adoption and sustainable digital transformation across Africa. 

To learn more or register to attend, visit www.aotlagos.com.

item.dc:creator: Israel Olaleye Toluwalope
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
In 2021, I graduated from the University of Ibadan with a degree in Mathematics. I thought my life would be about numbers on a whiteboard. I did not know it would become about numbers in people’s bank accounts, and the fears, hopes and contradictions that sit behind them.

By mid-2023, I had taken a job selling real estate. I started at the very bottom, as a sales development representative: the person who makes the first call, sends the message and follows up when nobody replies. Today, I manage a sales team. Somewhere between then and now, I stopped seeing real estate as a business of land and buildings. I started seeing it as a mirror. Put a property in front of a Nigerian, and you will learn, very quickly, how they think about money.

Here is some of what that mirror has shown me:

A prospect once told me, with complete confidence, “I have my money ready for the land.” We fixed an inspection. We walked the site together under the afternoon sun, red earth on our shoes. Then, standing on the plot, the prospect asked if they could pay next year. I was not angry. I understood. Saying “I am ready” feels good. Being ready is different. It means you have decided what the money is for, and you are willing to let it go.

I have seen versions of that moment many times. The client who books an inspection for 2 pm and is still not there at 4 pm. The person who asks for options, receives ten properties that match exactly what they requested, and replies, “Do you have something else?” The buyer who is ready until it is time to decide, and then needs three more months to think. The one who disappeared after asking for a price came back after the price went up, and asked for the old price.

For a long time, these moments frustrated me. But they taught me that most people do not have a money problem. They have a decision problem. We are a generation that earns, spends, plans and postpones, often all at the same time.

You can earn a lot and still not be wealthy

One idea I keep returning to is that you can earn twenty million naira a year and still not be wealthy. Income is what comes in. Wealth is what stays and grows. Two people can earn the same salary and end up in completely different places ten years later, simply because one converted part of that income into assets and the other converted all of it into lifestyle.

Wealthy people do not always look wealthy. Some of the most financially secure people I have met do not drive the loudest cars. And some of the people who look the richest are one bad month away from panic.

So the question I now ask myself, and the people I speak with, is simple: what exactly are you converting your income into?

Real estate is bigger than land and a house

One conversation changed how I explain property to people. A Nigerian living in Canada called me after watching a video I had made about a commercial development in Ibadan. A few minutes in, he said something I have since heard from many people: “To me, real estate has always meant two things. You buy land and keep it, or you build a house to live in.”

That is how many of us were raised to think about property. Land is pride. A house is security. Both are good. But they are only part of the picture.

Some assets are for appreciation. Some assets are for cash flow. Land grows in value while you wait, but it does not pay you while you wait. A shop, a rental apartment or a short-let can pay you while it grows. When I explained this, the whole conversation changed. We stopped talking about a single plot and started talking about a plan.

Not long after, I had almost the same conversation with another Nigerian abroad. He had never considered property as something that could produce income. He liked what he heard. He even had a deposit ready. But he planned to buy more than a year later. I had to tell him honestly that the option he liked might not be there by then. The right asset rarely waits for our calendars.

Patience is not the same as understanding

Another lesson came from buyers who purchase property with a five-year plan and then become anxious when the value has not doubled in eight months.

I used to think the answer was simply to tell people to be patient. Now I think the real mistake is not impatience. It is entering an investment without knowing what you are waiting for. Is it a road under construction? A growing population? New businesses moving in? If you do not know what should drive the value, every month of waiting feels like a loss.

Don’t just trust. Verify

The hardest lesson is about trust. Many Nigerians abroad send money home and leave a relative to handle everything. The intention is love. But love is not a process. Money gets misused. Documents are not checked. Sites are not visited.

My advice is never to stop trusting family. It is to stop relying on trust alone. Have a lawyer who checks the title. Have a surveyor who confirms the land. Let family monitor. And yes, check the consultant too, including people like me. Professionals can be dishonest. Don’t just trust. Verify.

I would rather a client ask me ten uncomfortable questions before buying than discover after payment that there was something they should have checked. Closing a deal is good. Knowing that the person understood exactly what they were buying is better.

What I am building

When I started, I thought success in sales would be measured by how many properties I sold. I still care about that. But I care more now about something harder to count: whether the people I speak with make better decisions with their money because of the conversation we had.

I want to keep learning, keep growing and keep building something that means more than a sales record. And I will say it plainly, the way I sometimes say it to myself on difficult days: watch out for a few years when you hear my name.

Not because I will have sold the most land. But because I hope my name will stand for something many Nigerians are still searching for when it comes to money and property: honest guidance, good judgment and trust that is earned, not assumed. The mirror is still there. Every inspection, every delayed payment, every late-night call from abroad shows me something new. And the biggest thing it has shown me is that before people buy property, they need to understand their own relationship with money.

item.title: From “Behind The Scenes” to “Call of My Life”: 5 All-Time Highest-Grossing Nollywood Movies
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
From Funke Akindele’s record-smashing "Behind The Scenes" and "A Tribe Called Judah" to Toyin Abraham’s "Oversabi Aunty" and the mid-year hit "Call of My Life," these five blockbusters redefined commercial success across Nigerian cinemas.

The post From “Behind The Scenes” to “Call of My Life”: 5 All-Time Highest-Grossing Nollywood Movies appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Toyin Abraham’s directorial comedy drama Oversabi Aunty is now streaming on Netflix and Kava.

Nigerian cinema has witnessed an unprecedented commercial evolution over recent years, with local box office totals soaring past figures once considered unthinkable. From the era when a four-hundred-million-Naira milestone set the nationwide ceiling to an era defined by multi-billion-Naira theatrical runs, audiences across West Africa continue to show up in massive numbers for homegrown storytelling.

Here is a look at the five highest-grossing Nollywood blockbusters in history that have continually redefined theatrical success, shattered industry records, and set historic commercial benchmarks across Nigerian cinemas.

A Tribe Called Judah (2023) — Domestic Box Office: ₦1.40 Billion

When this family heist drama landed in Nigerian cinemas on 15 December 2023, few anticipated just how dramatically it would reset the financial ceiling for homegrown features. Directed by Funke Akindele and Tobi Makinde for the Funke Ayotunde Akindele Network (FAAN), the story follows Jedidah Judah—played by Akindele herself—and her five sons from different fathers as they scheme to rob a luxury furniture shop to fund their mother’s life-saving medical care. Supported by a stellar lineup including Timini Egbuson, Jide Kene Achufusi, Uzee Usman, Tobi Makinde, Olumide Oworu, Nse Ikpe Etim, and Genoveva Umeh, the narrative struck a deep chord across multiplexes.

By the end of its theatrical run, the project had earned over ₦1.40 Billion, making history as the very first Nollywood title to surpass the ₦1 Billion domestic milestone and cementing Funke Akindele’s status as a formidable box office power.

A Tribe Called Judah poster celebrating its historic ₦1 Billion box office milestone. Photo Credit: Filmone/Instagram

Everybody Loves Jenifa (2024) — Domestic Box Office: ₦1.88 Billion

FAAN Studios returned to the festive release window on 13 December 2024 with a comedy-drama co-directed by Funke Akindele and Tunde Olaoye. Centred on the enduring popularity of the lead character, the narrative charts Jenifa’s latest misadventures across global settings, societal expectations, and personal choices, bolstered by on-screen performances from Falz, Layi Wasabi, Patience Ozokwor, and Stan Nze.

Building rapidly on its festive debut, the feature went on to generate ₦1.88 Billion in local ticket sales. The milestone surpassed Akindele’s previous commercial record and established an extraordinary streak of back-to-back record-breaking theatrical hits.

Funke Akindele and Falz on the ₦1 Billion milestone poster for Everybody Loves Jenifa. Photo Credit: Funke Akindele/Instagram

Oversabi Aunty (2025) — Domestic Box Office: ₦1.17 Billion

Toyin Abraham made her big-screen directorial debut with this comedy-drama from Toyin Abraham Films, which opened in cinemas nationwide on 19 December 2025. The plot introduces Toun, an overzealous church usher and self-styled neighborhood moral authority whose relentless meddling in family and community affairs triggers widespread hilarity and domestic chaos. Abraham leads an ensemble cast alongside Mike Ezuruonye, Lateef Adedimeji, Mercy Aigbe, Odunlade Adekola, Femi Adebayo, and Efe Irele.

Finishing its run at ₦1.17 Billion, the project set a career-high theatrical record for Toyin Abraham, making her the second filmmaker in Nigerian cinema history to steer a feature past the ₦1 Billion threshold.

Toyin Abraham and cast members on the ₦1 Billion milestone poster for Oversabi Aunty. Photo Credit: Filmone/Instagram

Behind The Scenes (2025) — Domestic Box Office: ₦2.76 Billion

Arriving in cinemas on 12 December 2025, this festive satire from FAAN Studios, co-directed by Funke Akindele and Tunde Olaoye, takes an unfiltered look at the ambition and internal friction governing the film industry. The story centers on Aderonke Fernandez—portrayed by Scarlet Gomez—a wealthy real estate mogul whose generosity is continually exploited by her extended family until she decides enough is enough. Akindele stars alongside an expansive cast featuring Tobi Bakre, Uzor Arukwe, Uche Montana, Destiny Etiko, and Ini Dima-Okojie.

The release made immediate history by crossing half a billion Naira within twelve days, before going on to break every existing West African box office record. It became the first Nollywood movie to cross the ₦2 Billion barrier, topping all-time theatrical rankings with a total gross of ₦2.76 Billion.

Funke Akindele on the milestone poster for Behind The Scenes after crossing ₦2 Billion.

Call of My Life (2026) — Domestic Box Office: ₦902 Million

Directed by Dammy Twitch, written by Uzoamaka Power, and produced by Blessing Uzzi under Bluhouse Studios, this romantic comedy was released in cinemas on 15 May 2026. The story follows Soluchi, a heartbroken call-centre agent whose life takes a sharp turn when a routine customer call with a charming presenter named Eli rekindles her belief in love. The cast stars Uzoamaka Power alongside Andrew Yaw Bunting, Beverly Osu, Zubby Michael, Broda Shaggi, Nkem Owoh, and Patience Ozokwor.

The project completely redefined non-festive box office expectations by becoming the highest-grossing mid-year release outside the traditional December festive window. It crossed the ₦600 Million mark faster than any non-December release in Nollywood history, finishing its theatrical run at ₦902 Million and outperforming legacy blockbusters like Battle on Buka Street and Omo Ghetto: The Saga.

The stars of Call of My Life gather for the film’s Lagos premiere. Featured from left are Andrew Bunting, Uzoamaka Power, veteran actor Nkem Owoh, producer Blessing Uzzi, director Dammy Twitch, and actress Beverly Osu. Photo Credit: Uzoamaka Power/Instagram

item.content:encoded:
Some people spend years trying to avoid awkward situations. Seyi Ademeso has built a career out of creating them, in the identity of Meshkiey. The content creator has turned everyday social discomfort into a distinctive style of comedy, earning an audience that recognises him for his unconventional approach to skits.

But there is more to Seyi than the character who seems willing to embarrass himself for a laugh. Beyond the camera, he is a creative strategist, entrepreneur and businessman with ambitions that stretch far beyond social media. In this exclusive, we sat down with him to talk about the journey, the person behind the persona and what he hopes to build next.

Hello Meshkiey. How are you feeling today?

I’m feeling good. Honestly, I’m grateful. I’m excited to have this conversation and reflect on the journey.

Before Meshkiey became the person people know online, what were you like growing up? 

I think I’ve always been a very observant person. Even growing up, I noticed little things about people, the way they behaved, the way they spoke, the funny things people did without realising they were funny.

I was also quite expressive. I wouldn’t necessarily say I was the loudest person in every room, but I definitely had a personality. I liked making people laugh, and I enjoyed doing things differently.

Looking back, I think a lot of the things people now associate with Meshkiey were actually already there. The difference is that I eventually found a platform where I could turn those traits into something creative.

When did you start creating, really? 

I started creating around 2016, and honestly, there wasn’t some grand master plan behind it. I think I just wanted to create. I had a phone, I had ideas, and I was fascinated by what people were doing online. At the time, content creation wasn’t necessarily viewed as a serious career path the way it is today.

My early content was very different from what people know me for now. I was experimenting a lot, trying different formats and figuring out what felt natural to me. I didn’t have the polished understanding of branding or storytelling that I have today.

I was basically learning in public. I was creating, posting, seeing what people responded to and slowly discovering my voice.

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Seyi Ademeso (@meshkiey)

Your seemingly awkward and creative style has become a character of its own. When did you realise that the things that might normally be considered unconventional could actually become your creative strength?

I think the realisation came gradually. At some point, I noticed that the things I thought were too awkward, too embarrassing or too unconventional were actually the things people remembered.

Instead of trying to fit into what I thought a content creator should look like, I started asking myself, “What if I lean completely into this?”

That became Meshkiey.

The awkwardness stopped being something I needed to hide and became a storytelling tool. I realised I could take an everyday human behaviour, exaggerate it, put myself in an uncomfortable situation and make people laugh because, somewhere inside, they recognised themselves in it.

That’s when I understood that being different wasn’t necessarily a disadvantage. It could actually be the brand.

Is there ever a point when you’re making a skit/content and you feel like “Nah, I can’t do this,” or has Meshkiey, as a character, shielded that part of you?

Absolutely. There are definitely moments where I’m standing somewhere and thinking, “What exactly am I about to do?”

But I think Meshkiey has given me a bit of freedom. The character comes with a level of shamelessness because once I decide on an idea, I’m willing to commit to it. And sometimes the funniest part isn’t even the joke itself; it’s watching me put myself through an incredibly awkward situation with a completely straight face.

So yes, Seyi sometimes thinks, “This is crazy.” Meshkiey says, “Let’s do it.”

So how much of Seyi is actually in Meshkiey?

A lot. Meshkiey is exaggerated, but he’s not fake.

The humour, the awkwardness, the observation, the willingness to do something ridiculous–those things are genuinely me. What I do for the camera is amplify certain parts of my personality. Seyi is probably more reserved and thoughtful in certain situations, while Meshkiey is like, “Let’s make this as awkward as possible and see what happens.”

So I wouldn’t say Meshkiey is a completely different person. He’s really just Seyi with the volume turned up.

What does a day in your life look like?

My days are honestly quite chaotic because I wear a lot of hats. There’s the content creator side of me, where I’m thinking about ideas, shooting, editing, meetings and brand campaigns. Then there’s the creative strategist side, where I’m working on campaigns, digital strategy, brand communication and helping businesses figure out how to communicate with their audiences.

I also run a greenery somewhere in Lekki, Lagos, CLASSYFLOWERY, so there’s a business side to my life that people don’t always see.

What has creating content taught you about yourself that school or a traditional career probably couldn’t have taught you?

Content creation taught me that there isn’t always a straight path to success. I studied International Relations at Covenant University, and I also have a diploma in French, so technically I could have followed a very conventional career path.

But content creation taught me how to build something from almost nothing. It taught me communication, marketing, storytelling, negotiation, resilience, business and, probably most importantly, how to understand people.

It also taught me that you can be talented and still fail. You can make something you love, and nobody cares. You can have a great idea and execute it badly. And that’s okay.

You learn, adjust and keep moving. I think that’s one of the biggest things the internet has taught me: You don’t necessarily need someone to permit you to start building the career you want.

What has been your proudest moment of your journey so far? Are there also challenges you’re trying to overcome?

I think my proudest moment isn’t one particular award or one particular number. It’s the fact that something I started experimenting with years ago has become an actual career and a recognisable identity.

The audience growth, the awards, working with major brands and seeing people recognise Meshkiey without me having to explain who I am–all of those things mean a lot.

But I’m also proud that I’ve been able to evolve beyond just being the person in front of the camera. I’ve become a strategist, producer, creative and entrepreneur.

The challenge now is growth without losing the originality that got me here in the first place. When people start expecting a particular version of you, it can become easy to play it safe because you know what works. I’m still trying to push myself creatively while building something sustainable beyond just social media.

If we have a conversation again five years from now, what would you like to be able to say you’ve done that would make you feel, “Yes, this is what I was working towards”?

Five years from now, I want to look back and feel like I didn’t waste the opportunity I had. I want Meshkiey to become bigger than just a social media personality. I want to build intellectual property around the character, create bigger productions, work across different forms of entertainment and continue developing as a creative.

I want Meshkiey to be recognised beyond Nigeria. I want to have created bigger projects, worked with incredible people and built things that have a life beyond Instagram or TikTok.

When the cameras are off, and there is no audience to entertain, what does Seyi Ademoso want for his life?

When the cameras are off, Seyi wants a good life. I want peace. I want meaningful relationships. I want to be able to take care of the people I love. I want to travel, experience things, build businesses and have the freedom to make choices without constantly worrying about survival.

And I want to be proud of the person I’ve become, not just because people know Meshkiey, but because Seyi himself is happy with the life he’s built. I think that’s the real goal. The internet sees Meshkiey. People see the funny guy, the awkward guy, the guy willing to embarrass himself for a video.

But at the end of all of that, I’m still just Seyi. And I want Seyi to have a life that is just as fulfilling when nobody is watching.

 

***

All photos culled from Seyi Ademeso’s Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
Daily Lagos–Asaba and Asaba–Abuja services resume on Friday, 20 November 2026, strengthening regional connectivity and bringing families together for the holidays.

Somewhere in Lagos or Abuja right now, a phone is ringing, and the voice on the other end is asking the single question that marks the true beginning of the Nigerian festive season: “When are you coming home?”

For thousands of professionals, business owners, and families whose answer is Asaba and the surrounding communities across Delta and Anambra states, ValueJet has delivered timely news. The airline will officially resume daily scheduled flights on its Lagos–Asaba and Asaba–Abuja routes starting Friday, 20 November 2026, just as year-end travel planning reaches peak momentum.

The end of the year carries an undeniable emotional pull back to one’s roots. It is the season of growing gift lists, overpacked suitcases, group chats buzzing with reunion itineraries, and the quiet warmth of returning to familiar streets. For many families, December represents the single period in the year when loved ones assemble under one roof.

By reintroducing daily non-stop frequency on both routes, ValueJet provides critical operational flexibility for holiday travelers. Whether passengers are heading home early to spend the entire season with family or flying out closer to Christmas Eve after wrapping up the work year, the restored schedule ensures seamless travel options tailored to diverse holiday schedules.

“The festive season is fundamentally about people, relationships, and shared moments. At ValueJet, our mission is to ensure that distance never stands in the way of those connections,” said Omololu Majekodunmi, Managing Director of ValueJet. “Restoring our daily services to Asaba reflects our deep commitment to serving the travel needs of our passengers during the most important time of the year. We are proud to offer a reliable, comfortable, and affordable gateway home for families and communities across the region.”

The Lagos–Asaba service bridges Nigeria’s commercial capital directly with the vibrant heart of Delta State, facilitating easy access across the South-South and South-East regions. Simultaneously, the Asaba–Abuja route delivers a direct, hassle-free link between the nation’s capital and Asaba, eliminating lengthy road journeys and complex connection itineraries.

The resumption complements ValueJet’s rapidly expanding domestic and regional network. Domestically, the airline provides essential air links to key destinations including Port Harcourt, Jos, Owerri, Calabar, Benin, and GWI-Iperu. Beyond Nigeria’s borders, ValueJet continues to extend its reach beyond established destinations like Accra, Banjul, Cotonou, and Malabo with upcoming regional route expansions to Libreville, Monrovia, and Abidjan.

To mark the relaunch and assist families with holiday travel planning, travelers are encouraged to book early to secure preferred travel dates.

For flight schedules, fare quotes, and online reservations, visit ValueJet’s official booking portal at www.flyvaluejet.com or contact customer service via official brand channels.

About ValueJet

ValueJet, operated by FlyForValue Aviation, is a premier Nigerian scheduled carrier dedicated to providing safe, reliable, and value-driven air transport. Founded in 2018 and launching commercial operations in October 2022, the airline operates out of its primary hubs in Lagos and Abuja. ValueJet connects key domestic commercial centers while expanding its regional footprint across West Africa—with routes covering Accra, Banjul, Cotonou, and Malabo. Driven by a modern fleet expansion strategy, ValueJet continues to redefine regional connectivity through exceptional service delivery and operational integrity.

Let’s talk about something plenty of us know too well. It is rarely the talent that is missing. You have been dancing since secondary school. You have been on the decks for years. You have been painting walls that people stop to photograph. The talent is there.

What is missing is the room. The one where somebody with reach finally looks up and goes, oh.

American Cola Club Talent is back for season two, and this year the theme says the quiet part out loud: Make Dem See.

Entries open 6th November 2026. But first, can we talk about last season?

If you were following in 2025, you’ll remember Show Your Flow. Five weeks. Talents from rap, dance, street art, disc jockeying, basketball, skating and BMX. Ten finalists. One winner.

That winner was DJ Mafdee Bitrus Moses Bugama. Fourteen years of showing up, reading crowds, and moving people before a platform like this came along. He went home with ₦1.5 million, a year of music streaming, a year’s supply of American Cola, media interviews, and a community impact project that American Cola funded completely.

Temz BusyTm (@temz_the_dj) came in as first runner-up, and dancer Adetutu (@_therealadetutu) took second place. And when the voting got tough? He went outside and asked people for votes one by one, because the rules allowed one vote per day. That is the kind of hustle and determination we love to see.

So what does “Make Dem See” actually mean?

Season one asked you to show your flow. Lovely. Season two goes one step further.

Make Dem See starts from the assumption that you are already good — and turns the attention to the people who haven’t noticed yet. The campaign film features four creators across dance, skating, DJing and street art, all of them talented, all of them tired of waiting to be discovered.

Sound familiar? Then this is your sign.

Now, the rewards (we know you scrolled here first)

  • ₦2,000,000 in cold, hard cash
  • A community impact project in your own city, fully funded by American Cola (Another 2 million naira)
  • Media features and interviews on national platforms
  • A full year’s supply of American Cola
  • Awards, medals and other gift items

Runners-up won’t go home empty-handed either — 200,000 naira in cash prizes and gift items.

How to enter American Cola Club Talent 2026

It is genuinely this simple:

  1. Film yourself doing your thing. Vertical, under 40-60 seconds.
  2. Post it on Instagram, Facebook, or TikTok and tag American Cola in your video. Use the hashtags #MakeDemSee and #AmericanColaClubTalent.
  3. Get your people ready for voting
  4. Follow @americancolanigeria for details

No manager needed. No follower count needed. No connections needed. Just you and whatever you are great at.

Why we are rooting for this one

Nigeria is not short of gifted young people. What we have always been short of are platforms willing to put real money and real structure behind them; and then keep showing up after the announcement post.

So if you have been waiting for a sign to finally put your talent in front of people, this is it.

Go and make dem see.

Like the flick of a finger, 2026 is coming to an end. It all feels like an hour ago when we wished each other “Happy New Year” and “Welcome to 2026.” Each month flew by, days folding into weeks, weeks folding into months, and here we are in November, preparing for December, Christmas, January, and a brand new year: 2027.

As it is tradition, the best way to close out the year is through reflection. A lot has happened this year, and with the few days remaining this year, a lot will still happen. Despite the many faces of 2026, the ups and downs, Nigerians and Africans showed up on big stages to express their creativity and talent. It was this year that Nora Awolowo and Damilola Osikoya broke the Guinness World Record for the largest attendance at a film screening with the screening of Black Market: The Movie. It was in 2026 that Ogaga Ifowodo won the $100,000 Nigeria Prize for Literature. It was in 2026 that Kayinsola Ajayi broke Nigeria’s 100m record. And many many more.

At BellaNaija, it was an even greater and more remarkable year. We celebrated our 20th anniversary with a Grand Red Carpet Experience. It was a beautiful evening that marked and solidified BellaNaija’s contribution as one of the culture shapers in Africa. Beyond the red carpet experience, it was the year of stories. We told stories of Africans and Nigerians achieving incredible feats at home and abroad. We told stories of educational success, stories of love, of Africans across the world. We did only what we are meant to do, and what we know best to do.

So we want to hear from you too. We want to know how 2026 has been for you. Did you start a new job? Did you find love? Did you start a new hobby or routine? Did you buy something you’ve always wanted? How were your finances? What experience from the year stood out for you? What did you manage to achieve? What did you fail to achieve? Share any experiences that brought you down, but also taught you how to pick yourself back up.

We want to hear about it all. We want you to write all about it.

Reflect on moments when you wished you had made different choices. Share instances where you chose to trust your intuition. Tell us about the beautiful experiences you had this year. We invite you to share your victories and setbacks, as well as your joys and sorrows, with us.

You have a lot to get a lot off your chest, and we are also ready to read, so share with us.

item.content:encoded:
With Earth & Sky, her Spring/Summer 2027 collection, Banke Kuku turns to nature’s most essential cycle: the sky gives rain, the rain feeds the earth, and the earth gives back. Reimagining the water cycle as a circle of life, the collection celebrates the abundance that flows from it. 

Earth & Sky is built around seven prints in three families. The Sky family is led by the hero print, Bougainvillea Sky, with watercolour bougainvillea, bees, butterflies and birds drifting across a turquoise ground, alongside Dove Sky and Daybreak Sky. 

The Earth family, Yellow Trumpet and Flower Bud, draws on flowering plants such as Costus spectabilis. The Rain family pairs Raindrop, a glossy, near-photographic print set against the softness of the watercolours, with the Kuku Monogram in fresh colourways. Sky prints are finished with hand-embroidered clouds and raindrops on flowing kaftans and kimono robes. 

Speaking on the inspiration, Creative Director Banke Kuku shares: 

“I never start with a sketch. I start with a feeling, and for Earth & Sky, that feeling was abundance. This year I became a mother for the first time, and everywhere I looked, nature was reflecting that same fullness back at me. This is my most personal collection.” 

A CYCLE OF GIVING BACK 

In nature, nothing is wasted, and everything returns. Earth & Sky carries that principle as its message: what we take from the earth, we must give back. That principle extends into how Banke Kuku approaches production. 

The brand maintains a no-waste policy, finding uses for offcuts rather than discarding them, while its seasonless approach allows pieces to remain part of the collection beyond a single season. Banke Kuku also uses digital printing, which consumes less heat and water than conventional printing methods, and continues to reduce its use of man-made fabrics in favour of more conscious material choices. 

Its commitment to the natural world extends beyond its collections, including its work with the Nigerian Conservation Foundation and its Re-Green Movement, which supports afforestation and the restoration of Nigeria’s natural environment. 

SHOW AND AVAILABILITY 

Earth & Sky will be presented on November 11, 2026, and will be available from December 2026 at the Banke Kuku flagship on Victoria Island, Lagos, and through global stockists.

ABOUT BANKE KUKU 

Banke Kuku is a British-Nigerian designer celebrated as the Queen of Prints. Nature is at the heart of everything she creates: flowers, birds, skies, and landscapes from Nigeria, transformed into bold prints and intricate textiles. Recognised by Vogue and a recipient of the Women in Making award, she designs womenswear, menswear and home textiles that bring the beauty of the natural world into everyday life.

item.content:encoded:
Over 10,000 women gathered at the Landmark Event Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos, on October 31, 2026, for the fourth edition of FinTribe Finance Fair, a growing movement dedicated to helping African women move from financial awareness to wealth creation and ownership.

Themed I CAN and powered by returning lead sponsor Sycamore, the event brought together financial experts, business leaders, entrepreneurs and influential personalities, including Funke Akindele, Omoni Oboli, BamBam, Sola Adesakin and Olufemi Shobanjo, for a day of practical financial education, inspiring conversations and meaningful opportunities.

For FinTribe founder Jennifer Awirigwe, popularly known as Financial Jennifer, the fair represents a bigger mission: helping women gain the confidence and resources to take charge of their financial futures.

“Financial education is important, but knowledge must eventually become action. We want women to leave Finance Fair knowing that they can save, invest, grow their income, build businesses and take ownership of their financial future,” she shared ahead of the event.

Beyond Finance Fair, FinTribe is building a community where women learn about money and put that knowledge into practice. With a presence across 43 countries, the organisation has reached over 20,000 women through financial education, supported more than 5,000 women with capital market training and helped members collectively save and invest millions of dollars.

Through its Wealth Builders Academy, savings and investment community, real estate initiatives and recently launched FinTribe App, the organisation continues to create opportunities for women to build healthier financial habits, develop investment confidence and work towards long-term financial independence.

At the fair, award-winning filmmaker Omoni Oboli encouraged women to pursue their ambitions without neglecting their wellbeing, reminding them to take things one step at a time, prioritise rest and ask for help when needed.

During the Financial Clinic, Sola Adesakin challenged women to become more intentional about their finances, emphasising the importance of earning, budgeting and turning income into real assets. She also introduced the four forces of money: Earnings, Expenses, Engines and Encumbrances.

Olufemi Shobanjo of NGX Regulation Limited shared insights into capital market participation, while actress BamBam, marketing strategist and Woof Studios founder Adetutu Laditan, and Mercy Agbeti, popularly known as Christian Money Woman, contributed to conversations about building value, navigating opportunities and growing with purpose.

One of the most memorable moments came during Funke Akindele’s session when a medical doctor and founder of Raffia Fashion Africa presented the actress with a pair of handcrafted raffia earrings.

Funke immediately wore them, danced, invited the entrepreneur onto the stage, embraced her, prayed for her and publicly endorsed her business.

The entrepreneur later shared on her instagram page that “she had saved to purchase a VIP ticket to the fair and had admired Funke for years”. What began as a simple audience interaction became a powerful demonstration of how visibility, encouragement and one meaningful connection can open doors for a growing business.

Beyond the stage, women connected with financial institutions, explored investment opportunities and participated in financial education sessions. The fair also featured empowerment opportunities and giveaways, including children’s investment portfolios, stock units, a plot of land, a Zanzibar trip and getaway experiences supported by partner organisations.

Sycamore returned as lead sponsor for the second consecutive year, alongside other partners supporting FinTribe’s mission to expand women’s access to financial knowledge and opportunities.

From its first edition in 2023 to this year’s gathering, FinTribe Finance Fair has continued to demonstrate the power of bringing women together around a shared goal.

But the real work continues long after the event ends. Through education, community, partnerships and practical wealth-building initiatives, FinTribe is helping women across Africa move beyond conversations about money to making informed decisions, building assets and creating financially secure futures.

To learn more about FinTribe, explore its programmes and join its growing community, visit www.thefintribe.com  or follow @thefintribe on Instagram.

item.content:encoded:
There’s something special about a collaboration that brings together music and visual art, particularly when both creatives have spent years helping African culture reach audiences around the world.

For its latest limited edition, Maison Martell has brought together Nigerian music superstar Davido and Ghanaian visual artist Prince Gyasi to create a new expression of its prestigious XO cognac, inspired by the sound, movement and global influence of Afrobeats.

The Martell Afrobeats Limited Edition XO will be unveiled in Nigeria on November 6, following the collection’s global launch in New York on October 28.

At the heart of the collaboration is Prince Gyasi’s distinctive artistic language. Known for his vibrant colours and imaginative compositions, Gyasi has created an original artwork of Davido that features on the limited-edition bottle and presentation box.

The design draws inspiration from the landscapes of West Africa, bringing together Martell’s iconic blue with shades of amber and gold. The blue reflects the rhythmic flow of the ocean, while the golden tones evoke sunlit sands and the warmth of African sunsets. Reimagined through Gyasi’s distinctive, hyper-surreal visual style, these elements create a composition that captures the movement and energy of Afrobeats while celebrating the unity, strength and creative spirit of the continent.

For Gyasi, the inspiration goes beyond the visual appeal of the bottle. Growing up in Ghana, his experience of music and its ability to bring people together informed the creative direction of the collaboration.

“Growing up in Ghana, I’ve seen firsthand how music brings people together, sparking connection, celebration, and pure joy. As Davido says, ‘We rise by lifting others,’ a reminder that music builds community and lifts us all. I feel a deep pride in Afrobeats, its incredible journey, and the mark it’s making on global music,” Prince Gyasi said.

He further explained the thinking behind the colours and composition: “Inspired by the landscapes of West Africa, I blended Martell’s iconic blue with the rhythmic flow of the ocean, golden sands, and waves reimagined in a hyper-surreal style, bringing sound and movement to life. Shades of amber and gold capture the warmth of African sunsets and speak to the continent’s unity, strength, and deep spirit.”

The result is an artwork that positions the limited-edition XO as more than a presentation of the cognac itself. It offers a visual interpretation of Afrobeats and recognises the artists and communities whose creativity has helped the genre travel across borders and influence audiences globally.

The project also reflects Martell’s five-year relationship with Davido, whose career has developed alongside the international growth of Afrobeats. Bringing Prince Gyasi into the collaboration introduces another creative perspective, connecting music and contemporary African art through a shared celebration of African expression.

Speaking about the collaboration, Davido described his partnership with Martell as an opportunity to continue pushing African culture forward, while Prince Gyasi’s creative contribution translates the energy, confidence and movement of Afrobeats into a visual experience.

Beyond the artwork, the limited-edition XO brings together Martell’s craftsmanship and a creative story rooted in African identity and contemporary expression. The collaboration also extends into Davido’s music video for Already Falling, filmed at Château de Chanteloup, Martell’s historic estate in Cognac, where the limited-edition collection makes an appearance.

The Nigerian unveiling on November 6 will be marked by an intimate dinner with Davido and Prince Gyasi, bringing together invited guests to experience the collaboration firsthand.

As Afrobeats continues to influence music, fashion, art and popular culture, the Martell Afrobeats Limited Edition XO is another reminder of how far the movement has travelled and the creative possibilities it continues to inspire. Through Davido’s music and Prince Gyasi’s visual storytelling, Martell celebrates a genre that continues to shape how African creativity is experienced around the world.

About Pernod Ricard Nigeria

Established in 2012, Pernod Ricard Nigeria is a member of the Pernod Ricard Group, a worldwide leader in the spirits and champagne industry, blending traditional craftsmanship, state-of-the-art brand-building, and global distribution technologies.

Our prestigious portfolio of premium to luxury brands includes Inverroche Gin, Absolut vodka, Ricard pastis, Ballantine’s, Chivas Regal, Royal Salute, and The Glenlivet Scotch whiskies, Jameson Irish whiskey, Martell cognac, Havana Club rum, Beefeater Gin, Malibu liqueur, Mumm and Perrier-Jouët champagnes.

Our mission is to ensure the long-term development of our brands with full respect for people and the environment while empowering our employees around the world to be ambassadors of our purposeful, inclusive, and responsible culture of authentic conviviality.

About Martell

Founded in 1715 by Jean Martell, Maison Martelll is the oldest of the great cognac houses and a symbol of audacity, mastery, and refinement. For over three centuries, Martell has celebrated those who dare to move differently, guided by curiosity, courage, and the pursuit of excellence. At the heart of the House stands The Swift, Martell’s timeless emblem of freedom, vision, and forward motion. It represents a spirit that never stands still, a commitment to rise above convention and redefine what refinement means in every era.

From the iconic Martell XO to the boundary-breaking Martell Blue Swift, every creation reflects a legacy of craftsmanship and an invitation to live boldly, purposefully, and with audacity. For more information, visit martell.com or follow @martellofficialnigeria

OBIMI CIC is a UK-based community organisation supporting parents and caregivers of children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). Its founder, Helen Ewumi, is a qualified social worker and a parent of children with disabilities. Her professional experience and family life both inform OBIMI’s commitment to helping families feel heard, supported and less alone.

The Nigeria outreach brought families together in Lagos to share experiences and raise awareness about the importance of understanding disability and challenging stigma.


Around 100 families received support through the outreach, including food hampers. Clothing was also shared with families.

During the visit, the OBIMI team went to a special school in Lagos and gave pupils school bags and stationery. These practical gifts were offered to support children with their learning and to remind them that they are valued and included.

The gathering also created space for families to connect and take part in conversations about disability. OBIMI’s message was clear: every child deserves to belong, and families should be met with understanding, respect and support.


For Helen, taking OBIMI’s work to Nigeria was an opportunity to connect with families and communities in Lagos. As a social worker and a parent with lived experience of caring for children with disabilities, she understands how important it is for families to feel listened to and supported.

OBIMI CIC is grateful to the families, school staff, volunteers, partners and supporters who helped make the outreach possible.

The organisation hopes to continue building connections and raising awareness so that children with disabilities and their families can feel seen, supported and included.

OBIMI founder Helen Ewumi at the Nigeria outreach in Lagos. A UK-based social worker and parent of children with disabilities, Helen founded OBIMI to support families and challenge disability stigma.

item.content:encoded:
One year and two months ago, I took a career pivot. I moved from being a digital media professional writing stories, articles and shaping narratives to becoming an analyst in the energy sector, working across the oil and gas and renewable subsectors.

The journey across these two industries that are worlds apart has taught me lessons on starting over

You are never really starting from scratch

No matter what you are starting over at or what you are getting into, it is important to realise that you are never truly starting from zero. Where ‘zero’ means the state of having nothing: skills, experience, network, intelligence, and others. While it may indeed appear that you do not have the things you consider as being critical to starting over, you actually have what you have: the knowledge, skills and experiences that have shaped your life and marked your journey up to this present moment, and this is invaluable.

Also, having a strong knowledge of yourself is also an incredible resource when starting over, as it helps you to discern and differentiate challenges that are due to your personality, and challenges that are due to the circumstance of starting over.

Your ‘Next Best Move’ is hidden within your network

When we think of network, it is easy to limit it to close friends, relatives or even acquaintances. This is quite a restrictive and limiting view of the concept of network. Your network also includes ‘strangers’ and your internet community.

In my case, I knew of the opportunity in the energy sector through a friend whom I had met on Instagram. It gets more interesting. By the time I was preparing for my first interview, I knew that I had zero knowledge about the current state of the sector. Thanks again to Instagram, I reached out to someone I followed who I knew worked in the sector, and she offered a free virtual coffee chat. I went into the interview more confident in what value I could offer and what mattered for such a role.

Transferable skills are invaluable

Prior to my career pivot, my only exposure to the energy sector aside from buying fuel and gas was a seminar paper I had written in my final year investigating annual shifts in fuel pump prices. However, I audited my skills and qualifications and noted that I also had highly transferable skills. I had communication, business development and a good knowledge and expertise in using Canva. For you, it could be international exposure, multiple languages or something else you think is insignificant. 

No matter what you are starting over at, you have something that can be transferred from where you were to where you are or where you want to be.

Adopt a growth mindset

In today’s world, flexibility, adaptability and agility are your currencies for greatness. A critical part of thriving through a transition, a pivot or when you are starting over is to be honest about your limits. These could be the limits of your existing knowledge, expertise, and others. 

However, recognition alone is not enough; you need to have a radical belief in your ability to grow. As you seek to start over, it is imperative that you understand that every industry, sector, phase or environment has its own unwritten rules of engagement. Develop cultural intelligence, build on the skills you need, and take the posture of a student: learn, unlearn and relearn from everyone and everywhere. Reframe failure as a learning curve and continue to chart your own unique course in your life’s journey.

item.content:encoded:
Nancy Isime‘s first film as executive producer, from GREOH Studios, is a beautifully shot story about the love that holds a family together when life falls apart.

Some films you watch. Others stay with you. Loving Itohan is the second kind.

It opens like the love story you think you already know: a radiant bride, an Edo wedding, coral beads and gold everywhere. You settle in for romance. Then, slowly, the film shows you its heart, and it is so much bigger than a love story.

At its centre is Itohan, played by Nancy Isime, a woman whose world is shaken by loss and by truths she never saw coming. What follows is a story about grief, the quiet kind that stays in a home long after the visitors have gone. It is about family, the people who hold us up and sometimes weigh us down. And it is about love that has to keep choosing to stay, even when it hurts.

You will see yourself in it. In the person trying to hold everyone together. In the things left unsaid at the dinner table. In the slow, uneven way healing actually happens.

A film that looks as good as it feels

The cinematography deserves its own round of applause. Every frame feels deliberate, from the rich reds and golds of Edo tradition to the close, quiet moments where a single look says everything. The camera knows when to celebrate and when to simply sit with a character in her pain. This is a film made for the big screen.

There is a reason it all feels so assured. Loving Itohan is from GREOH Studios, and Jade studio has never been afraid to go big, with daring, genre-bending stories like Gangs of Lagos. This time, GREOH goes deep instead, trading spectacle for the messy, tender feelings we all carry. True to form, it also hands the director’s chair to a fresh talent, Orobosa Ikponmwen, the latest in a line of new directors the studio has backed, from Kayode Kasum to Loukman Ali. And for Nancy Isime, this is her very first project as an executive producer. You can feel how much of herself she has poured into it, in front of the camera and behind it.

Alongside her, Uzor Arukwe, Martha Ehinome Orhiere, Dorathy Bachor, Grace Dein Coker, Chioma Nwosu, Florence Sunday and newcomer Obehi Aburime bring the family to life.

Don’t judge it by the trailer

If the trailer has you thinking you know where this is going, trust us, you don’t. Go with someone you love. Bring tissues. And maybe call your mum afterwards.

Loving Itohan is in cinemas nationwide from 6 November 2026.
